analysis.one_liner: Replaces employer health coverage with tax credits, medical savings accounts, and guaranteed-issue private plans while loosening antitrust rules for hospitals.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to four committees and never received a markup or a vote, dying when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have unwound the employer-based health insurance system. It would end the tax break for employer-provided insurance and instead give individuals a refundable tax credit for health costs, create tax-favored medical savings accounts, and require employers to cash out their health contributions as wages. It would then require every state to certify private "federally qualified" plans that must take all applicants, renew coverage, and cap out-of-pocket costs — while preempting state benefit mandates and shielding hospital mergers and provider joint ventures from antitrust law.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, uninsured and low-income households would have gained a refundable, advance-paid tax credit for premiums, and people with preexisting conditions who kept continuous coverage would have gained guaranteed issue and renewal. Insurers would have gained a new subsidized individual market, banks and insurers new tax-favored savings accounts, and hospitals broad antitrust safe harbors for mergers and joint purchasing. Younger and healthier buyers would have paid less under age-based premiums.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The uninsured, insurers, hospitals, and banks

how_it_helps.text: Creates a refundable tax credit for health premiums and out-of-pocket costs, tiered at 22%, 44%, or 66% depending on how large the expense is relative to income, with the credit advanced through employers during the year so cash-strapped families don't wait for tax season.

Requires insurers to issue and renew coverage for all applicants, and to cover preexisting conditions for anyone continuously insured for at least a year, with a break-in-coverage exclusion capped at one year.
Caps out-of-pocket costs at the greater of $5,000 or 10% of family income for plans covering acute care, physician services, hospital care, and inpatient prescription drugs.
Standardizes claims forms and electronic medical data to cut administrative costs, and adds criminal penalties plus whistleblower rewards of up to $10,000 for health care fraud.

analysis.who_pays: Older adults and women, since premiums could vary by age and sex; people incurring up to $5,000 or 10% of income in out-of-pocket costs; workers who would lose the bargaining power of employer group plans and be switched to individual policies; the Treasury, which would replace the employer tax exclusion with credits; and states, which would lose authority over insurance benefit mandates and managed-care rules.
analysis.who_pays_short: Older and sicker patients, workers, and states

drawbacks.text: Premiums could vary by age, sex, and geography, so older people and women would pay far more in the individual market than under community-rated employer group coverage.
The out-of-pocket limit is the greater of $5,000 or 10% of family income — a family earning $60,000 could owe $6,000 before coverage fully pays.
Title IV exempts hospital mergers, provider joint ventures, joint purchasing, and collective negotiations from antitrust laws, allowing consolidation that could raise prices for patients.
Federal law would preempt state laws requiring coverage of specific services and state restrictions on managed care, stripping protections states had enacted.

Terminating the exclusion for employer-provided insurance, the self-employed deduction, and the medical expense deduction would be one of the largest tax changes ever, forcing a disruptive one-time conversion of group plans into individual coverage.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs genuine consumer protections — guaranteed issue, guaranteed renewal, and out-of-pocket caps — with provisions that shift risk onto individuals: age-and-sex rating, a high out-of-pocket minimum, weakened antitrust enforcement for hospital consolidation, and the dismantling of employer group purchasing in a single step. An honest reading is that the guaranteed-issue protections were the strongest part, while the antitrust exemptions and the abrupt end of employer coverage could have raised costs for older, sicker, and female enrollees and reduced competition among hospitals.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to four committees and three subcommittees, none of which ever held a markup or vote, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. Cliff Stearns introduced the bill on April 6, 1995, with three Republican cosponsors.
The same day, it was referred to four committees: Ways and Means, Commerce, Judiciary, and Rules.
Within three weeks it was sent to subcommittees — Health, Health and Environment, and Rules and Organization — and no further action of any kind was taken.
The bill never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or a Senate companion action, and died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died quietly, the existing employer-based system and state-by-state regulation stayed intact: employers avoided the mandated cash-out of health benefits, and insurers avoided guaranteed-issue requirements — while the uninsured and people shut out of the individual market gained nothing at all.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and insurers; the uninsured gained nothing

for.name: Rep. Cliff Stearns
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it through referral to four committees.

against.name: Chair Bill Archer, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: The Ways and Means Committee never held a markup or reported the bill after it was referred and sent to its Health Subcommittee.

against.name: Chair Thomas Bliley, House Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: The Commerce Committee never acted on the bill after referral to its Health and Environment Subcommittee.

against.name: House leadership of the 104th Congress
against.role: Majority leadership controlling the floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor; with no committee action, no vote could occur before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so no party split is recorded; all four supporters on record — the sponsor and three cosponsors — were Republicans, and no Democrat cosponsored.

industries.note: The bill makes private certified plans the permanent channel for all health coverage: tax credits flow only through federally qualified plans, and MSAs create new products for banks and insurers. In exchange, insurers would face guaranteed issue, guaranteed renewal, and rating restrictions they did not otherwise have in the individual market.

Title IV shields hospital mergers, high-tech joint ventures, joint purchasing, and provider negotiations from antitrust laws, letting providers consolidate and bargain collectively — consolidation that tends to raise the prices patients pay.

Employers would be relieved of sponsoring and negotiating health coverage, ending their role as purchasing agents for workers, though they would have to add the cash value of their former contributions to wages. Workers lose the group-plan bargaining power and risk pooling that came with it.

industries.industry: Banks and financial firms offering medical savings accounts
industries.note: Tax-exempt medical savings accounts with a 25% contribution credit (capped at $3,000 plus $500 per dependent) would create a new trust and custodial-account business, though mainly useful to households with spare cash to set aside.
Federal law would preempt state mandated-benefit laws, anti-managed-care laws, and cost-sharing restrictions, stripping state consumer protections in exchange for a federally defined floor.
